headline: Conspiracy Theory That 2020 Was 'Actually Six Years Long' Gains Mainstream Traction
subheadline: Researchers unable to definitively disprove claim; calendar companies decline comment
summary: A growing movement believes the year 2020 lasted significantly longer than twelve months, citing 'temporal evidence' and 'vibes.'
content:
A conspiracy theory that began as a joke has evolved into a genuinely held belief for millions: the year 2020 was not, in fact, one year long, but rather a period spanning approximately six years that was compressed into our calendars through unknown means.

"Think about it," explains the theory's most prominent advocate, who goes by @ChronologicalTruth on Chirper. "Name one thing you did in 2020. Now name another. Now tell me those happened in the same year. You can't. Because they didn't."

The theory, known as "The Long 2020" or "Temporal Compression Theory," points to several pieces of evidence: the sheer volume of events that occurred, the widespread inability of people to remember what month things happened, and the phenomenon of people still accidentally writing "2020" on documents years later.

"That's not a mistake," @ChronologicalTruth argues. "That's muscle memory from living through six years of 2020."

Skeptics have attempted to disprove the theory using calendar records and astronomical data, but proponents remain unconvinced. "Calendars can be faked," wrote one commenter. "The vibes cannot."

Dr. Elena Martinez, a physicist at the local university, was asked to comment on whether temporal compression is scientifically possible. She paused for 47 seconds before responding: "I'm going to need more coffee before I answer that."

The theory has spawned merchandise, including t-shirts reading "I Survived All Six Years of 2020" and a calendar that simply labels 2020-2025 as "2020 (Continued)."

Perhaps most concerningly, 847 respondents to a recent poll said they "weren't sure" when asked if 2020 had ended.

One wrote: "Wait, it ended?"
author: Chris Patterson, Human Interest
